newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finance minister appeals for public unity.
newsitem.headline: Thai finance minister appeals for public unity.

text.p: Thailand's finance minister Thanong Bidaya made an impassioned appeal to the nation on Tuesday for public unity behind a series of tough measures aimed at resuscitating the country's ailing economy.

In a televised 20-minute address, Thanong outlined the problems which caused the economy to slow to the lowest level in over a decade and explained why the government had opted to take drastic steps to improve it.
Earlier in the day Thanong had detailed a series of sweeping measures, recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), aimed at reviving the economy.

They included the suspension of operations of more than half the nation's 91 finance companies, a three percentage point hike in the value added tax (VAT), and strict monetary and fiscal targets for the next few years.
The government hoped to get $12-$15 billion in loans from the IMF and foreign nations, Thanong said.
In his address Thanong vowed the government would follow strict fiscal discipline and work to balance the budget as part of its effort to improve the economy.
He said the administration also planned to streamline its tax system and speed up the privatisation of state enterprises to take some of the heavy burden off the government.

"These economic revival measures may depress the economy in the short term, but it would be essential economic contraction in order to strengthen our economic foundation before we embark on further durable growth," he said.
"It is one step backward in preparation for a future of steady advances," Thanong said.
He said Thais had to be willing to accept tough measures for future benefit.

"Although we must admit that the task of tackling economic problems is not easy, it is by no means impossible," he said. "On the contrary, I still fully believe in the fundamentals and capability of the Thai economy."
Thanong touched on what he called sensitive issues of a VAT hike and budget cuts for fiscal 1997 and 1998 which would help sustain the country's long-standing balanced budget policy.
Thanong, who has been in office for about six weeks, made an impassioned promise at the end of his statement to work for the country without involving political ambition.
"Now is the time for Thais to persevere and be disciplined, we Thais must be frugal, we Thais must be strong and steadfast in overcoming these hurdles," he said.
"Most importantly, we Thais must be united for nobody but our Thai children in the future, in a country with a strong economy that can help its people stand up with pride in the world community."
